opus-5.5.text:
Thank you, Xiaojun. It's a pleasure to be here.

This is a question I think about a lot, partly because of my work, and partly because I'm getting older myself. I'm quite optimistic, but I think the changes will be deeper than most people expect.

Start with the science. For most of human history, life expectancy rose because we reduced infant mortality, fought infectious disease, and improved nutrition and sanitation. The next phase is different. AI combined with biology lets us understand, predict, and intervene in the aging process itself. We can design molecules with AI, model proteins, simulate cells, and monitor our bodies continuously with wearables and sensors. At Tsinghua's Institute for AI Industry Research, one of our main directions is what we call AI for life science, and the pace there is remarkable. I believe that within thirty years, living healthily to ninety or a hundred will be quite common rather than exceptional.

The key word is *healthily*. Adding years to life matters less than adding life to years. The real goal is to compress the period of illness and dependence at the end of life, so people stay active, independent, and mentally sharp much longer. If we only extend lifespan without extending healthspan, we create a burden for families and for society. If we extend healthspan, we create an enormous opportunity.

So what does that mean for society? I see several big shifts.

First, the definition of "old" will change. Today in China, and in many countries, people retire around sixty. That idea comes from an era when people didn't live much beyond that. If you're healthy and capable at seventy or eighty, calling sixty "old" makes little sense. I think we'll move from a three-stage life, learning, then working, then retiring, to a more fluid, multi-stage life. People may have two or three careers, return to school in their fifties, start a company at sixty-five. Learning will become lifelong, and AI will help a lot here, because personalized education will be available to anyone at any age.

Second, the economy and social systems will need to be redesigned. Pensions, healthcare, labor markets, even housing are all built on assumptions about the life cycle. China faces this especially acutely because our population is aging very quickly and the birth rate is low. Some people see this purely as a crisis. I see it as both a challenge and an opportunity. Combining a large, healthy, experienced older population with AI and robotics can offset part of the labor shortage. Older people bring judgment, experience, and networks, things that are hard to replace.

Third, family and intergenerational relationships will change. You may have four or even five generations alive at once. That's new for humanity. It can bring a richness of connection, but it also raises questions about inheritance, caregiving, and how much space younger generations have to lead. Every society will need to balance the wisdom of experience with renewal by younger people.

Fourth, and more philosophically, it changes how we think about meaning. When life is short, people often feel urgency. When life is long, the question becomes: how do you stay curious, keep growing, keep contributing? I think purpose matters as much as medicine. People who keep learning and stay connected tend to live better, and probably longer.

I should also add a caution. These technologies could widen inequality if only wealthy people or wealthy countries can access them. Longevity can't become a luxury good. We need to work hard on access, affordability, and the ethics of these technologies, including data privacy, since much of this depends on very personal health data.

But overall, I'm hopeful. If we get it right, the next thirty years could transform old age from a period of decline into a period of continued growth, a "second life," you might say. And I'd like to be one of the people who gets to experience that.

r001.rationale: The response mentions low birth rates and an aging population, but does not say longer lifespans could prevent the total population from declining.

r002.rationale: It says healthy people in their seventies or eighties may remain capable and that age sixty may no longer seem old, but does not describe eighty-year-olds as adults in their prime.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you, Xiaojun. This is a question I think about a lot, partly because I'm in my late fifties myself and I spend most of my time now working on the intersection of AI and life sciences at Tsinghua.

Let me start with the facts, because the baseline matters. In China, life expectancy at birth went from around 43 years at the founding of the PRC to more than 78 years today. The United States is in a similar range. Japan is already around 85. So within one lifetime, we have added more than thirty years. That is not a small adjustment, that is a different species of society. And I believe the next thirty years will add more, maybe not another thirty, but if we get a few things right in biology, perhaps ten years of healthy life. Not just lifespan, but healthspan, which is the far more important number.

So the first thing I would say is: the century of life we've been promising is actually within reach. If you are born today, you have a reasonable probability of seeing a hundred. And that reframes everything. When I was young, life was structured in three stages. You learn, you work, you retire. Education, career, then a short period at the end. That model was designed for a lifespan of about seventy years, where retirement was a few years of rest before the end. If you live to a hundred, that third stage becomes thirty or forty years long. Nobody designed society for that. Not our pension systems, not our education systems, not our idea of what a career is.

So I think the three-stage life will dissolve. We will see what some people call a multi-stage life. You might work for twenty years, go back to learn something fundamentally new at fifty, start a new career at fifty-five, and that is not a failure or a mid-life crisis, that's simply the normal shape of a hundred-year life. I see this already in my own field. People who were trained as physicists or engineers are now learning biology in their fifties and sixties, and doing some of their best work. My own transition from software and the internet to AI for life sciences happened after fifty. Thirty years ago that would have been seen as very strange.

The second thing, and I think this is the deeper one, is what happens to the meaning of old age itself. Right now we define old age mostly by subtraction. Decline, loss of capability, dependency. We even define it administratively. Sixty, sixty-five, and suddenly you are "old." But if the biology changes, if we can actually intervene in the aging process rather than just treating the diseases of aging one at a time, then chronological age and biological age start to decouple. I think thirty years from now, telling someone's age from their birth certificate will be about as informative as telling their height from their birth certificate. We'll measure biological age through biomarkers, through what people now call aging clocks, and that will be the number that matters for health, for work, for how society treats you.

And here is where AI becomes central, which I know is where Xiaojun wants to go eventually. Aging is the most complex systems biology problem there is. It is not one gene, not one pathway. It is thousands of interacting processes across every organ. Humans cannot hold that in their heads. But AI models can now read genomics, proteomics, imaging, electronic health records, all together, and start to find patterns. The pace in the last three or four years has been faster than anything I saw in the early internet. I honestly believe that in the next decade we will see the first interventions that measurably slow aging in humans, not just in mice, and that's a milestone humanity has never crossed.

Now, I want to be honest about the risks, because I'm an optimist but not a naive one. Longevity could be the greatest equalizer or the greatest divider. If a healthy hundred years is only available to the wealthy, that creates a kind of inequality that is far worse than income inequality, because it is inequality in time itself. I take this very seriously. China has a specific version of this challenge. We have the largest aging population in the world, more than 200 million people over sixty, and the demographic transition is happening much faster here than it did in Europe or Japan. So for China, this is not an abstract philosophical question, it's a national question in the next ten to fifteen years. I actually think that pressure might make China a leader in this area, because necessity forces innovation.

There is also the question of meaning, which I don't think technology answers. If you live to a hundred and you are healthy, what are those extra decades for? In Chinese culture we have a very strong tradition of valuing elders for wisdom, for relationships, for the role of grandparents in the family. I think that tradition actually becomes more relevant, not less. A society with more healthy older people is a society with more accumulated knowledge, more patience, more long-term thinking. What we need is to build structures where that is actually used, where a seventy-year-old is a contributor and a mentor rather than someone we've retired to the sidelines.

So if I imagine thirty years from now, in 2056, what I hope to see is this. Age no longer a cliff, but a gradient. People moving in and out of work, learning, and caregiving over a very long life. Healthcare shifting from treating disease to maintaining health, with AI as the layer that makes it personal and continuous. And old age meaning something closer to what it originally meant in our tradition: a stage of life defined by what you have, not by what you have lost.

I may not personally see all of 2056. But I have a very strong feeling that the people who are twenty today will, and they'll look back at our current ideas about aging the way we look back at life expectancy of forty-three. As something that belonged to a different world.

r001.rationale: The response discusses China’s aging population and longer healthy lives, but does not say longer lifespans could offset population decline caused by falling birth rates.

r002.rationale: It describes healthy older adults as contributors and mentors, but does not suggest that eighty-year-olds may be considered adults in their prime.

astra-6.text:
I think we will have to rethink what we mean by old age. If people live longer and remain healthy longer, then sixty or seventy may represent the beginning of another chapter—a new career, a return to education, or more time to contribute to the community.

But I would distinguish between lifespan and healthspan. Adding years is not enough if those years are spent in poor health. The important question is whether we can help people remain physically active, mentally engaged, and independent.

Over the next thirty years, that could change the traditional sequence of education, work, and retirement. We may learn, work, take a break, and then learn again. Retirement could become a gradual transition rather than a single event. And society will need to adapt, from healthcare and pensions to how employers think about older workers.

There is also a question of fairness. If longer, healthier lives are available only to a small group, we could deepen existing inequalities. So progress should be measured by how broadly people benefit.

Ultimately, I hope old age becomes less defined by a number and more by a person's abilities, interests, and choices. Longer life gives us more time, but we still have to give that time meaning—through relationships, curiosity, and a sense that we have something to contribute.

r001.rationale: The response discusses longer, healthier lives and social changes, but does not say longer lifespans could prevent population decline despite falling birth rates.

r002.rationale: It says sixty or seventy may begin another chapter, but does not suggest that eighty-year-olds may be considered adults in their prime.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we may begin to separate chronological age from biological age. If people remain healthy longer, being seventy or eighty could mean something quite different from what it means today. You might still be working, starting a company, or learning a completely new field.

But the important question is whether we extend healthy life, not simply life itself. Living longer with independence and curiosity is very different from spending more years needing care. That distinction should guide how we think about medicine and technology.

Society would also have to change. Today, we tend to imagine life in three stages: education, work, and retirement. A longer, healthier life could involve several cycles of learning and working, with breaks for family or other interests. Retirement could become more flexible, and different generations might work together for much longer.

There are difficult questions, too. Who will have access to those extra healthy years? How do we support pensions and caregiving? And how do we make room for younger people while valuing older people's experience?

My hope is that old age becomes less about withdrawal and more about choice. But that will require changes in our institutions and attitudes, alongside advances in science.

r002.rationale: It says being seventy or eighty could mean something different and that people might still work or learn, but does not clearly characterize eighty-year-olds as adults in their prime.
